summary:
Montana stands under the legal framework of the United States, and separately under a state constitution whose equal-protection and dignity guarantees have repeatedly defeated anti-trans legislation in its courts. Legislation that would otherwise place Montana among the most restrictive states has not taken full effect, and in the July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment Montana is the only state whose standing improved, on the strength of that court record. Adult restrictions that were enacted remain unenforced pending litigation, while the youth-side picture stays unsettled through continuing federal policy shifts and court challenges.

Senate Bill 458, signed in May 2023, codified sex as an immutable male-female binary determined at birth and unchangeable. District Judge Leslie Halligan struck it down in February 2025 for violating the equal-protection clauses of the Montana Constitution, finding that it left a gap in sex-discrimination protection. Senate Bill 437, signed on 24 March 2026, re-enacted biological definitions of sex, gender, male, female, man, woman, mother and father keyed to primary sexual anatomy and reproductive system, and provides that gender means sex and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role. Those definitions reach more than 60 sections of state law, including driver's licences, marriage licences and anti-discrimination protections, and applicants for driver's and marriage licences must list sex as so defined. Representative Zooey Zephyr stated that the bill erases transgender, intersex and Two-Spirit recognition, and in April 2026 plaintiffs sought to add it to the ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to SB 458.

Identity-document changes have been restricted and blocked in alternating waves. On 9 September 2022 Montana prohibited changing sex identification on birth certificates absent proof of a data-entry error or a DNA test; a court order on 15 September 2022 blocked the rule and the Department of Public Health and Human Services complied. A bill signed on 19 May 2023 prohibited gender-marker changes on all identity documents and was blocked by a December 2024 injunction from District Judge Mike Menahan. Following an April 2024 suit by two trans women unable to update their driver's licences and birth certificates, Judge Menahan issued a preliminary block on 16 December 2024 on sex-discrimination grounds, which the Montana Supreme Court upheld on 15 April 2026, holding that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity.

A Helena district court reached the same position in December 2024, preliminarily enjoining enforcement of the 2022 health department rule barring gender-identity-based changes to birth-certificate sex, the Motor Vehicle Division policy requiring a birth certificate before a driver's-licence sex change, and portions of SB 458, on finding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on claims that the restrictions constitute sex discrimination violating the Montana Constitution's fundamental right to be free from sex discrimination. Enforcement is paused while that litigation continues. The prior sequence ran the other way: sex-reassignment surgery and clinical treatment were required until December 2017, when the surgery requirement was replaced by a correction affidavit, gender designation form, court order and doctor's letter for licences; an April 2021 law reintroducing surgical procedures and a court order, signed with immediate effect by Governor Greg Gianforte, was blocked in April 2022 for lack of clear legal definitions, after which the department imposed a temporary emergency rule in May 2022 banning updates and later made it permanent.

Facility use is governed by House Bill 121, passed in February 2025, which requires bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly funded facilities to be segregated by biological sex assigned at birth. The ACLU of Montana sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 District Judge Shane Vannatta temporarily restrained the law, ruling that it is motivated by animus and supported by no evidence that the restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. Two earlier attempts failed: a 2018 Montana Family Foundation initiative to require public bathroom use matching birth-certificate gender did not gather enough signatures for the ballot, and on 3 December 2024 the Montana House voted down a proposal to bar trans people from using Capitol bathrooms aligned with their gender.

Gender-affirming care for trans minors is not banned in Montana. Senate Bill 99, signed on 28 April 2023 and described as the most comprehensive such prohibition in the United States, was preliminarily enjoined on 27 September 2023 by District Judge Jason Marks, who held that discrimination against a person for being transgender is inherently sex discrimination under Bostock v. Clayton County and served no compelling governmental interest in protecting minors. The Montana Supreme Court kept the injunction in place on 11 December 2024 on privacy grounds, with Justice Laurie McKinnon adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class, and Judge Marks permanently struck the law down on 14 May 2025 for failure to establish a bona fide health risk clearly and convincingly or a change in the stance of major United States medical organizations.

A 2021 law barring transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on continued federal education funding and signed the following month by Governor Gianforte, was struck down in September 2022 by District Judge Rienne McElyea as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the Regents of the Montana University System.

Protection against discrimination is split across layers. By executive order Montana prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and by state contractors and subcontractors, a policy originating in 2000 personnel rules from Governor Marc Racicot, broadened in November 2008 by Governor Brian Schweitzer's Executive Order 41-2008 and extended to gender identity and contractors in January 2016 by Governor Steve Bullock. Federal Title VII protection for gender identity under Bostock v. Clayton County applies in Montana, and ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations, with Missoula County covering county employees only. Montana's hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, so prosecution falls to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009. In April 2021 Governor Gianforte signed legislation granting a right to discriminate where religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as a licence to discriminate against LGBTQ people.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised in Montana since 19 November 2014, when Judge Brian Morris enjoined the state ban effective immediately; the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015 mooted the question, and the Montana Supreme Court recognised a common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in Adami v. Nelson on 10 December 2019.
tangentialFactors:
Official symbolism is restricted. House Bill 819, debated on 6 March 2025 and signed by Governor Gianforte in May 2025 with immediate effect, prohibits flags representing political party, race, sexual orientation, gender or political ideology on government property and in public schools, which bans Pride and other LGBTQ flags. Official historical flags remain permitted, including the Gadsden flag, law-enforcement and Thin Blue Line flags, tribal nation, foreign country, military service branch, POW/MIA and official school or government entity flags.

Public performance by gender-nonconforming people was targeted in May 2023 by House Bill 359, which prohibited sexually oriented or obscene performances in public spaces where minors may be present and explicitly barred drag story hours at publicly funded schools and libraries. A Butte-Silver Bow library cancelled a transgender woman's reading in response. District Judge Brian Morris issued a temporary restraining order in July 2023, extended in October 2024, blocking enforcement as vague and overbroad with a risk of disproportionate enforcement against trans, Two-Spirit and gender-nonconforming people. A March 2025 bill, HB 675, defining drag as inherently sexual was defeated with 13 Republicans joining Democrats.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Montana since 1997, when the Montana Supreme Court held in Gryczan v. State that the prohibition on same-sex sexual contact between consenting adults was unconstitutional; the enjoined provision was legislatively repealed on 18 April 2013. The prior 1973 code had renamed sodomy as deviate sexual conduct, applicable only to same-sex conduct and punishable by up to ten years' imprisonment and a 50,000 dollar fine, with a 1989 law requiring registration with the local chief of police.

Montana's improvement in the July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment is a ranking of state legal environments rather than a measure of incident counts, and it reflects unenforced statutes rather than their repeal: the underlying laws remain on the books should the injunctions lapse.
localsOnly:
Residents have additional state-level protections and gaps. State statutes do not directly address sexual orientation discrimination, but executive orders bar it in state employment and contractors, from 2000 rules by Governor Racicot, November 2008 Executive Order 41-2008 by Governor Schweitzer and a January 2016 expansion by Governor Bullock; federal Title VII protection for sexual orientation under Bostock v. Clayton County applies, and the Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish ordinances cover employment, housing and public accommodations. Montana's hate-crime statutes omit sexual orientation as well as gender identity, leaving prosecution to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act.

Montana permits adoption by individuals with no explicit prohibitions on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption. Kulstad v. Maniaci, affirmed 6-1 on 7 October 2009, granted parental rights and set precedent for stepparent adoptions by same-sex couples. Lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised if married, and surrogacy is unregulated, with courts generally favourable and issuing pre-birth parentage orders for genetic relationship and case-by-case orders without a genetic link.

In May 2025 House Bill 819's neutrality requirement was interpreted to prohibit Pride flags as official government displays, and Missoula adopted a rainbow pride flag as its municipal flag, a step treated as a loophole effectively exempting it statewide. A May 2021 parental opt-in law requires parental consent before K-12 sex education.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Senate Bill 437's definitions are operating while the April 2026 challenge proceeds is unresolved in the sources; the inventory records the filing seeking to add the bill to existing litigation but no ruling on it.

The final outcome of the document-marker litigation is unresolved. The sources record a preliminary injunction of December 2024 upheld on 15 April 2026 and a separate December 2024 Helena injunction pausing enforcement while litigation continues, but no trial judgment on the merits.

Whether House Bill 121 remains under restraint after the temporary restraining order of 2 April 2025 is unresolved; a temporary restraint is time-limited and the sources do not record a later order.

No trans-specific homicide or violence figures for Montana appear in the inventory, so no assessment of violence risk above the general Montana rate can be made from these sources. Whether federal charges were brought in any gender-identity-motivated case in the state is likewise not sourced.
